name: Alien Gambit
oneLiner: 1.e4 c6 … 6.Nxf7!? — sacrifice the knight on f7 and hunt the king. 👽 Engine says no, the 1500s say yes.
offBook: The hunt only works on the rails — {exp} keeps the king cornered.
Drift here and Black consolidates. {exp} keeps the fire lit.
Off the abduction route 👽 — {exp} is the move.

lines.name: Main King-Hunt (7…e6)
lines.idea: Objectively a knight down — Stockfish gives Black ≈ −2.7. But f7 is shattered, the king is stranded in the centre, and below ~1500 White scores around 60%. Pure chaos: Black has to find only-moves to survive.

done: A knight down and winning — that’s the Alien Gambit.

moves: 5…h6 — “shooing” the knight, straight into the trap.
6.Nxf7!? — the Alien Gambit. The fork on d8/h8 makes …Kxf7 forced (else the queen falls to Nxd8).
7.Bc4+ — drag the king into the open; the checks begin.
8.Qf3 — pile on f6 and e6 (Qxf6+ and Bxe6+ loom). The king has no shelter.

lines.name: King retreats (7…Ke8)
lines.idea: If Black scurries the king back to e8 instead of blocking, develop fast. Nf3, Ne5 and Qf3/Qe2 keep the king stuck in the centre with no castling and a lasting initiative for the piece.
moves: 7…Ke8 — retreating, but castling rights are gone for good.
8.Nf3 — the last piece; Ne5 and Qe2 keep the king in the crossfire.

name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.e4!? — sacrifice a pawn, rip open the f-file, and hunt the king.
offBook: You sacked the pawn for the initiative — {exp} keeps it screaming.
No half-measures in the BDG. {exp} keeps the f-file open.
That hands the pawn back for nothing — {exp} is the move.

lines.name: Teichmann (5…Bg4)
lines.idea: The main line. Black pins the knight; you take it off, develop Be3/O-O-O and play the open f-file. Black is a pawn up (≈ −0.5) but you have the bishop pair, the open f-file and a big lead in development — textbook BDG compensation, not a knockout.
moves: The gambit move — challenge d5 at once.
4.f3 — offer the pawn to open the f-file.
5.Nxf3 — the Blackmar-Diemer proper: open f-file, two tempi, Bc4 to come.
5…Bg4 — the Teichmann, Black’s most popular try.
7.Qxf3 — recapture toward the kingside; the queen eyes f7 and b7.
9.O-O-O — your tabia: castled long, bishop pair, open f-file and a development lead for the pawn. This is the BDG you want.

lines.name: Teichmann — 6…Bh5
lines.idea: If Black keeps the bishop, chase it with g4 and plant a knight on e5.
moves: 7.g4! — gain space and hit the bishop.
8.Ne5 — the monster knight; threats on f7 and g6 loom.

lines.name: Bogoljubow (5…g6)
lines.idea: Black’s safest reply. There is NO forced attack here — the Qe1–h4–Bh6 plan loses to …Bxh6. Play calmly: with best defence Black is a touch better (≈ −0.7), but the pawn buys real, lasting activity and practical chances.
moves: 5…g6 — the Bogoljubow, the soundest line for Black.
6.Bc4 — eye the f7-square along the open diagonal.
8.h3 — calm: deny …Bg4 and keep developing (8.Qe1?! Bh6 trades your attacker).
9.Be3 — finish development; pressure d4/centre, the pawn gives lasting play.
10.Bd5 — clamp the long diagonal; practical chances for the pawn (≈ −0.7).

lines.name: Euwe (5…e6)
lines.idea: Black’s solid main defence. Pin with Bg5, develop Bd3, castle, and lift the queen toward the kingside. Objectively Black is better (≈ −1), but you get a genuine, lasting attacking initiative for the pawn — the practical heart of the BDG.
moves: 8.O-O — bring the rook to the open f-file.
9.Qe1 — the lift toward h4 / h-file storm.

lines.name: Gunderam (5…Bf5)
lines.idea: Black develops the bishop outside. Hit it with Ne5 and a g4/h4 pawn-storm; the bishop gets buried.
moves: 6.Ne5 — central knight, eyes f7 and g6.
8.h4 — the pawn roller; the g6-bishop is in trouble.

lines.name: Ziegler (5…c6)
lines.idea: A flexible defence; meet …Bf5 with Ne5 and the same g4 storm.

lines.name: 5…Nc6 (Schlutter)
lines.idea: Black blocks the c-pawn. Gain space with d5 and the knight has to retreat awkwardly.
moves: 5…Nc6 — blocks the c-pawn, a slight inaccuracy.
7.Bf4 — challenge the knight, develop with threats.

lines.name: Ryder — Halosar Trap (5…Qxd4)
lines.idea: Sacrifice a SECOND pawn with 5.Qxf3. If Black grabs d4, the queen is hunted until she must give back a whole piece. White wins by force, ≈ +4.

done: Halosar nailed — that’s the whole trap. Filed away.
Textbook execution of the Halosar. Beautiful.
wrong: Careful — the Halosar only works move-perfect. It was {exp}.
Slip and the queen escapes for free. The move is {exp}.

moves: 5.Qxf3!? — the Ryder: offer the d4-pawn as bait.
5…Qxd4?? — grabbing the bait. Loses by force.
6.Be3! — attack the queen, the hunt begins.
8.h3 — squares running out for Her Majesty.
9.Bb5+ — check, dragging a pawn to c6.
10.Nge2! — heading for f4; the queen has no safe square.
10…cxb5 — the only way to save the queen is to hand back the bishop.
11.Nxb5 — material regained and a crushing attack. ≈ +4.
12.O-O-O — castle into the open files; the double sacrifice paid in full.

lines.name: Ryder — Queen Raid (5…Bg4)
lines.idea: The bishop hits your queen; ignore it and dive with Qxb7, snatching the queenside two pawns up.
moves: 6.Qxb7! — the raid. Snatch b7, eye the a8-rook. ≈ +0.3, sound.
7.Nf3 — calm development; the queen has escape squares.
8.Qxa7 — the queen strolls out two pawns up. 70%.

lines.name: Declined — Vienna (4…Bf5)
lines.idea: Black declines with …Bf5. Recapture e4, then the Qf3 double-attack (b7 and the e4-knight) forces …Nd6 and you regain the pawn with the easier game — fully equal and engine-sound (≈ 0.0).
moves: 6.Qf3! — double attack: the e4-knight and b7.
7.Bf4 — develop with pressure on the d6-knight.

lines.name: Declined — Langeheinecke (4…e3)
lines.idea: Black returns the pawn with …e3 to kill the gambit. Take it with the bishop — you get a free developing tempo and a fine game.
moves: 4…e3 — hand the pawn back to deny you the open f-file.
5.Bxe3 — a free developing move; you’re comfortable.
7.Nge2 — flexible; O-O and a kingside plan next.

lines.name: Declined — Lemberger (4…e5)
lines.idea: The sharp counter-gambit. Trade into a pleasant endgame where Black’s …e5 weakens him.
moves: 5.dxe5 — accept; Black’s queen comes out into the open.
6.Kxd1 — the king is fine here, the e5-pawn cramps Black.

lines.name: Declined — O’Kelly (4…c6)
lines.idea: Black supports d5/holds e4. Recapture and meet …e5 with quick development and queen trade into a comfy position.
moves: 7.Qxd4 — centralise; trade queens into an easy edge.

lines.name: Lemberger Countergambit
lines.idea: White offers a pawn with e4 and f3 for open lines and a quick attack. Objectively Black can hold, but the practical chances are big.

name: Benoni Defence
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 — the Benoni: hand White the centre, get a queenside majority and a raging dark-squared bishop.

lines.name: Classical Main (8.Be2)
lines.idea: The main Modern Benoni. Fianchetto, castle, and uncoil with …Re8, …Na6–c7 and the thematic …b5 break. Objectively White is a shade better (≈ +0.7), but it’s one of the richest, most double-edged structures in chess — you play for the win as Black.
moves: 6…g6 — the Benoni bishop heads to g7.
10…Na6 — reroute to c7 to support …b5; rich, fighting middlegame.

lines.name: Fianchetto (7.g3)
lines.idea: White fianchettoes to blunt your bishop. Develop solidly and aim for …Re8/…Na6 and the …b5 lever; the d6/c5 majority is your trump.
moves: 9…Na6 — the modern setup; …Nc7 and …b5 to come.

lines.name: Four Pawns Attack (7.f4)
lines.idea: White grabs the whole centre with f4. Meet the Bb5+ check with …Nfd7 (the main antidote), castle, and counter the over-extended pawns with …Na6 and …b5.
moves: 7.f4 — the Four Pawns Attack, the most ambitious try.
8…Nfd7! — the key move; the big centre becomes a target.

lines.name: Czech Benoni (3…e5)
lines.idea: Lock the centre with …e5. A patient manoeuvring game: reroute the knight …Ne8–g7 and prepare the …f5 break.
moves: 3…e5 — the Czech Benoni, a closed, strategic battle.

lines.name: Benko Gambit (3…b5)
lines.idea: Sacrifice a wing pawn for long-term pressure: the half-open a- and b-files and a powerful g7-bishop give lasting, low-risk initiative.
moves: Black has full compensation: the open queenside files and the long diagonal.

lines.name: Czech Benoni
lines.idea: Black gives White the centre but gets queenside pawn majority and the long diagonal for the g7-bishop. Sharp, double-edged.

name: Benoni Gambit
oneLiner: 1.d4 c5!? — offer the c-pawn. Take it back cleanly after 2.dxc5, spring a piece-winning trap if White clings to it, or get the sharp Old Benoni after 2.d5.
offBook: The trap only springs on the right move-order — {exp}.
Grab it back the clean way: {exp}.
Off the gambit script — {exp} is the move.

accepted.label: Accepted · 2.dxc5
accepted.blurb: White takes — you regain it (with a trap)

lines.name: Accepted Main (…e6 & …Bxc5)
lines.idea: White grabs the c-pawn — a dubious move that just loses time. Play …e6 and …Bxc5: you regain the pawn with a developing tempo and a comfortable, fully equal game (≈ +0.1). The clean way to refute the capture.

correct: Right — take the pawn back with tempo.
Clean. That pawn was never really White’s.

moves: 1…c5!? — the Benoni Gambit; offer the pawn.
2…e6 — prepare …Bxc5 to round the pawn up.
3…Bxc5 — pawn regained, bishop developed with tempo.
Fully developed and equal — the gambit has done its job.

lines.name: The b4 Greed Trap
lines.idea: If White clings to the pawn with the natural-looking 3.b4, punish it: …a5 cracks the queenside open and …Qf6 traps the a1-rook on the bared long diagonal. White loses a piece by force (≈ −2.7). The reason humans fear taking the pawn.

done: A whole piece — that’s why nobody should grab the c-pawn. 🪤
wrong: The trap is move-perfect — it was {exp}.
Slip and White wriggles out. The move is {exp}.

moves: 3.b4?! — greedily clinging to the extra pawn.
5.cxb4 — …and the a1–h8 diagonal is wide open.
5…Qf6! — the trap: the a1-rook has no defence down the open diagonal.
6…Qxc3+ — fork the king and the loose pieces; the greed costs a knight.
7…Qa3 — pocket the piece and consolidate. Winning.

lines.name: Quick Regain (2…Qa5+)
lines.idea: The simplest way to win the pawn straight back: …Qa5+ and …Qxc5. You concede a touch of time (≈ +0.5), but it’s clean and easy if you don’t want the …e6 theory.
moves: 2…Qa5+ — check, then …Qxc5 rounds up the pawn.
Pawn back, a slightly passive but solid game.

lines.name: Declined — Locked Centre (2.d5 e5)
lines.idea: If White declines with 2.d5, bolt the centre with …e5 (a Czech-Benoni shape). Honest: White gets a real space edge here (≈ +0.8 with the h4–h5 push) — an offbeat surprise weapon, not an equalizer.

lines.name: Declined — King’s-Indian Setup (2.d5 d6)
lines.idea: Against 2.d5, treat it like a King’s Indian: fianchetto, castle, and break with …e6 or …b5 against White’s big centre.
moves: 6…O-O — a KID-Benoni structure with …e6/…b5 to come.

name: Budapest Gambit
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5!? — sac a pawn for fast, active piece play and tricks on the dark squares.
offBook: The e5-pawn comes back by force — {exp} is how.
Lose the tempo and the gambit fizzles. {exp} keeps the pieces buzzing.
Off the dark-square plan — play {exp}.

adler.label: Accepted · Ng4
adler.blurb: The main road — win the pawn back

lines.name: Adler Main (4.Bf4)
lines.idea: The main line. Pin with …Bb4+, pile on e5 with …Qe7, and regain the pawn with a comfortable, active game.
moves: 2…e5! — the gambit; offer the pawn for activity.
3…Ng4 — hop back to round up the e5-pawn.
4.Bf4 — White clings to the extra pawn.
5…Bb4+ — develop with check and add a defender of …Ngxe5.
7…Ngxe5 — the pawn comes back; Black is fully equal and active.

lines.name: Rubinstein (…Bc5)
lines.idea: A sharper try: …Bc5 hits f2. White must watch the …Ng4xf2 and …Bxf2+ tricks while you round up e5.
moves: 4…Bc5 — train the bishop on f2; tactics loom.

lines.name: Alekhine 4.e4
lines.idea: White grabs the centre with 4.e4. Take on e5 at once and harass the big pawns with …Bb4+ and …d6.
moves: 4.e4 — the Alekhine line, a broad centre.

lines.name: Fajarowicz (3…Ne4)
lines.idea: The bold cousin: the knight leaps to e4. Quick development with …Bc5 and …Nc6 sets nasty tricks against an unprepared White.
moves: 6…d6 — strike back at e5 before White consolidates.

lines.name: Declined 3.d5
lines.idea: White locks the centre with 3.d5 instead of taking. Treat it like a Czech Benoni in reverse: clamp with …Bc5 and …d6.
moves: 6…Ng4 — provoke a weakening or trade dark-squared bishops.

lines.name: Declined 3.Nf3
lines.idea: White holds the centre with 3.Nf3. Push …e4 to gain space and chase the knight; Black gets a pleasant game.
moves: 3…e4 — gain space and kick the knight.

lines.name: Budapest Gambit
lines.idea: Black gives up a pawn on e5 but gets rapid development and chances for a quick regain with activity.

name: Caro-Kann
oneLiner: 1.e4 c6 — solid as granite: a sound structure, the good bishop out early, no weaknesses.

lines.name: Classical (4…Bf5)
lines.idea: Develop the light-squared bishop outside the chain to f5/g6, finish development cleanly, and stand rock-solid.

lines.name: Advance (3.e5 Bf5)
lines.idea: Unlike the French, the bishop escapes to f5 before …e6. Develop behind it and chip at d4 with …c5.
moves: No bad bishop — the Caro point.

lines.name: Panov–Botvinnik (Exchange c4)
lines.idea: White takes on d5 and plays c4 for an IQP game. Blockade d5, develop actively, and target the isolated pawn.

lines.name: Exchange (3.exd5)
lines.idea: The quiet Exchange. Get the bishop out to g4, meet Qb3 with …Qd7, and reach a comfortable, symmetrical game with no weaknesses. (≈ =)
moves: Calmly defend b7 — equal and solid.

lines.name: Caro-Kann Defense
lines.idea: Black prepares ...d5 with a pawn on c6, so the light bishop can develop outside the pawn chain. Safe, sound and good for endgames.

name: French Defence
oneLiner: 1.e4 e6 — solid and combative: a rock-solid chain, then break with …c5 and …f6.

lines.name: Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4)
lines.idea: Pin and trade on c3 to wreck White’s queenside pawns, then besiege the doubled pawns and the centre.
moves: Target the doubled c-pawns and e5.

lines.name: Classical (3.Nc3 Nf6)
lines.idea: Develop classically; after Bg5 trade dark-squared bishops and play against the cramped e5-chain with …c5/…f6.

lines.name: Advance (3.e5)
lines.idea: White grabs space with e5. Undermine the base of the chain with …c5 and …Qb6, hitting d4 and b2.
moves: Clamp the queenside and play on the light squares.

lines.name: Tarrasch (3.Nd2)
lines.idea: Against 3.Nd2, hit the centre at once with …c5; equal, active piece play in an open position.

lines.name: French Defense
lines.idea: Black accepts a cramped bishop on c8 for a rock-solid structure. The plan is to attack White's centre with ...c5, then play for counterplay.

name: Italian Game
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 — the oldest opening: target f7, then choose calm or carnage.

lines.name: Giuoco Pianissimo (c3/d3)
lines.idea: The modern Italian: a small centre with c3 and d3, castle, regroup Nbd2–f1–g3, and build a slow kingside attack.
moves: 4.c3 — prepare d4 and a slow build.

lines.name: Two Knights (3…Nf6 4.Ng5)
lines.idea: The aggressive 4.Ng5 hits f7. After …d5 you snatch a pawn and hold the extra pawn against Black’s initiative (≈ equal — Black has real compensation).

lines.name: Evans Gambit (4.b4)
lines.idea: A romantic pawn sac: deflect the bishop, grab the centre with c3 and d4, and come crashing at f7.
moves: 6.d4 — rip open the centre for the sac.

lines.name: Italian Game
lines.idea: The bishop eyes f7 and White builds with c3 and d3 or d4. Great for beginners because the ideas are simple and the development is natural.

name: Jobava London
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 — an offbeat, aggressive London. Objectively Black equalizes, but the Nb5 jumps and h4 storms force awkward play and score well below master level.
offBook: The teeth are in the plan — {exp} keeps Nb5 and h4 live.
Play it straight and it’s just a dull London. {exp} keeps the bite.
Off the storm — {exp} is the move.

lines.name: Nb5 Jump (3…e6)
lines.idea: The signature Jobava try: 4.Nb5 provokes …Na6 and dictates the setup. Honest: with best play Black is fine (≈ −0.3) — the knight reroutes via …Nb4 — but the awkward …Na6 trips up club opponents constantly.
moves: 3.Bf4 — the London bishop comes out before e3.
4.Nb5!? — eyeing c7 and d6; Black must react.
4…Na6 — defends c7, but the knight sits offside for now.
8.Nc3 — the knight returns. Roughly level (≈ −0.3): you’re playing for the practical awkwardness of Black’s Na6, not an objective edge.

lines.name: Classical 4.e3 Bd6
lines.idea: Black challenges the bishop with …Bd6; you keep it with Bg3 and recapture toward the centre, opening the h-file.
moves: 7.hxg3 — recapture toward the centre; the h-file is yours for the attack.

lines.name: Anti-Nb5 (3…a6)
lines.idea: Black spends a tempo on …a6 to stop Nb5. Just build the London setup — it’s roughly level, with the extra …a6 a small practical plus for you.

lines.name: Early …Bf5
lines.idea: Black mirrors with …Bf5. Play f3 and e4 to blast open the centre while Black’s bishop is offside.
moves: 5.e4! — the central break, the whole point of f3.
7.Bd3 — a big pawn centre and the bishop pair pointed at the king.

lines.name: Aggressive …c5
lines.idea: Black strikes with …c5. You grab it and jump Nb5, but Black recaptures cleanly with …Bxc5 and is comfortable (≈ −0.5). Play it as a sharp, fighting game — not a free pawn.
moves: 4.dxc5 — grab it; the pawn comes back, but you get a lead in development.
5.Nb5!? — heading for d6, hitting the loose dark squares.
8.Nbd4 — Black is comfortable (≈ −0.5); play actively for the initiative, the pawn was always coming back.

lines.name: h4 vs …g6
lines.idea: Against the fianchetto, the Jobava bayonet: h4–h5 to pry at the king. Double-edged and very practical — sound for Black, dangerous over the board.
moves: 5.h4!? — the bayonet; meet …h5 with a sharp game, or storm with h5 yourself.

name: Queen's Gambit
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 — the classical bid for the centre; meet every defence with a clean main line.

accepted.label: Accepted · 2…dxc4
accepted.blurb: Black takes; you take the centre

declined.label: Declined · 2…e6
declined.blurb: The QGD — Black holds the centre

lines.name: QGD Main (4.Bg5)
lines.idea: The classical QGD. Pin with Bg5, trade off on d5, and play with the slightly freer game and the c-file.
moves: 4.Bg5 — the classical pin on the f6-knight.
11.Rc1 — pressure down the half-open c-file; a tiny, durable edge.

lines.name: QGD Exchange (Minority Attack)
lines.idea: Trade on d5 early and launch the minority attack: b4–b5 to gouge a weakness on c6.
moves: 4.cxd5 — the Exchange; fix the structure for a queenside plan.

lines.name: Cambridge Springs (6…Qa5)
lines.idea: Black’s tricky …Qa5 hits the pinned knight. Calmly unpin with Nd2 and the pin backfires.
moves: 6…Qa5 — the Cambridge Springs, eyeing the pin and c3.
7.Nd2! — unpin and defend; the queen sortie loses its sting.
9.Be2 — calmly finish development with a comfortable game.

lines.name: QGA Main (3.Nf3)
lines.idea: Don’t rush to regain the pawn — develop, recapture on c4, and enjoy a free, central game.
moves: 3.Nf3 — stop …e5 first; the pawn isn’t running away.
9.Nbd2 — a pleasant edge in a queenless middlegame.

lines.name: QGA Central (3.e4)
lines.idea: The ambitious 3.e4 grabs a big centre at once. If Black hits it with …e5, don’t rush to regain d4 — develop and hit f7/b7 with Qb3, standing clearly better (≈ +1.1).
moves: 3.e4 — the central QGA, a broad pawn front.
7.Qb3! — hit f7 and b7. Not 7.Nxd4?? Qxd4 (the d4-knight has two attackers, one defender — Black wins a piece). White is clearly better.

lines.name: Slav Main (5.a4 Bf5)
lines.idea: Black keeps the c8-bishop active with …Bf5. Clamp with a4, regain the pawn on c4, and develop smoothly.
moves: 5.a4 — stop …b5 and prepare to round up c4.

lines.name: Semi-Slav Meran (7…b5 8.Bd3)
lines.idea: The Meran: let Black grab queenside space, then blow open the centre with e3–e4.
moves: 9.e4! — the Meran break; a rich, fighting centre.

lines.name: Tarrasch (3…c5)
lines.idea: Black accepts an isolated d-pawn for activity. Fianchetto with g3/Bg2 to blockade and press d5 long-term.
moves: 6.g3 — the Rubinstein system; the bishop will eye d5.
9.Bg5 — pile up on the isolated d5-pawn.

lines.name: Chigorin (2…Nc6)
lines.idea: Black’s offbeat …Nc6. Take the bishop pair, prop the centre with e3 (note: e4? drops d4 to …Nxd4), and the doubled f-pawns are a small price (≈ +0.5).
moves: 2…Nc6 — the Chigorin, piece play over structure.
5.gxf3 — grab the bishop pair; the doubled f-pawns are fine.
6.e3 — solid: defend d4 first (6.Nc3? Qd6 7.e4?? Nxd4 wins the pawn).
9.bxc3 — two bishops, a broad centre, the long-term pull.

lines.name: Albin Counter-Gambit (2…e5)
lines.idea: A gambit reply. Take on e5, blockade the advanced d4-pawn, fianchetto, and just be up a pawn.
moves: 5.g3 — the modern antidote; bishop to g2 and round up d4.
8.O-O — castled, a clean extra pawn, no counterplay.

lines.name: Baltic (2…Bf5)
lines.idea: The …Bf5 sideline. Take on d5, win the bishop back with the Qa4+/Rxb1 trick, and emerge with the bishop pair and a pleasant space edge (≈ +0.5).
moves: 2…Bf5?! — developing the bishop before …e6 traps it in.
3.cxd5 — the bishop on f5 is now loose.
4.Qa4+! — the in-between check that rounds the bishop up.
7.b4 — grab queenside space; a comfortable, lasting edge.

lines.name: Queen's Gambit
lines.idea: White challenges d5 with the c-pawn. If Black takes, White regains the pawn and gets a strong centre; if not, White keeps a space advantage.

name: Ruy Lopez
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 — the Spanish: pressure the knight, the centre, and squeeze.

lines.name: Closed Main (Morphy)
lines.idea: The classical Spanish: retreat the bishop to b3, brace the centre with c3/h3, and build a kingside bind.

lines.name: Exchange (4.Bxc6)
lines.idea: Trade on c6 and play the better pawn structure: four vs three on the kingside in the endgame.

lines.name: Berlin Defence (3…Nf6)
lines.idea: The Berlin Wall. Steer into the famous queenless endgame where your structure and the bishop pair give a nagging pull.

lines.name: Open Spanish (5…Nxe4)
lines.idea: Black grabs e4 for activity. Hit back with c3 and a timely d4-build; the centre and bishop tell.

lines.name: Ruy Lopez
lines.idea: The Spanish is the classic main road: pin the defender of e5, castle, and build up the centre step by step. Slow squeeze, rich in plans.

name: Scotch Gambit
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 — sac the centre pawn for a screaming initiative on f7. Sound, sharp, and full of traps.
offBook: The gambit lives on the initiative — {exp} keeps the fire on f7.
Slow down and the pawn just matters; {exp} keeps it sharp.
Off the attack — {exp} is the move.

lines.name: Classical 4…Bc5 5.c3
lines.idea: The main line. You sac a piece with 9.d5! for a raging attack and full compensation — engine-perfect, it’s dynamic equality (≈ 0.0) but a nightmare for Black to defend.
moves: 4.Bc4 — the Scotch Gambit: develop and aim at f7 instead of recapturing.
5.c3 — challenge the d4-pawn and open lines.
7.Nc3 — the sharp choice; block with the knight.
8.O-O — ignore the pawns, get the king safe and the rook to e1.
9.d5! — the point: sac the piece, hit the Nc6, and open everything.
10.Re1 — pin the e4-knight to the king.
11.Rxe4 — win the knight back; you’re a pawn down with a crushing initiative (≈ 0.0).
12.Bg5 — pile on the pins; full comp and a dangerous attack.

lines.name: 4…Nf6 5.e5
lines.idea: If Black develops with …Nf6, kick it with 5.e5 and regain the pawn with Nxd4. A normal, sound game (≈ equal) — no fireworks, just a pleasant Italian-style centre.
moves: 5.e5 — gain space and chase the knight.
6.Bb5 — pin the c6-knight before it’s defended.
10.Be3 — develop, trade if invited; a balanced middlegame (≈ equal).

lines.name: Max Lange Attack
lines.idea: The legendary Max Lange: 6.e5! and a forced storm down the e-file and at f7. Engine-approved — White is a touch better (≈ +0.2) with a ferocious initiative.
moves: 6.e5! — the Max Lange Attack; the f6-knight is hit.
8.Re1+ — the check that powers the attack.
9.Ng5 — hit the pinned bishop on e6.
10.Nc3 — develop with tempo on the queen.
White is slightly better (≈ +0.2) with a raging attack; Nxf7! is in the air.

lines.name: Greedy 5…dxc3 — Bxf7+ trap
lines.idea: If Black gets greedy and grabs 5…dxc3, punish it: 6.Bxf7+! rips open the king. After the forced sequence White is clearly better (≈ +0.7), Black castle-less and exposed.
moves: 5…dxc3? — too greedy; the second pawn costs Black the king’s safety.
7.Qd5+ — fork the king and the Bc5.
8…d6 9.Qxc3 — material is level but Black has lost castling and is passive (≈ +0.7). Develop and attack.

lines.name: Solid 4…Be7
lines.idea: Black sidesteps the fireworks with …Be7. Just take the pawn back with Nxd4 and enjoy a comfortable, better centre (≈ +0.4) — no gambit needed.
moves: 5.Nxd4 — no need to gamble; regain the pawn with a fine position.
8.h3 — tuck the bishop’s retreat in; White is comfortably better (≈ +0.4).

lines.name: Advance Variation
lines.idea: Instead of recapturing, White develops the bishop and castles, aiming at f7 while Black's pieces are still at home.

name: Sicilian Defence
oneLiner: 1.e4 c5 — the fighting answer to 1.e4: unbalance the game and play for the win as Black.

anti.label: Anti-Sicilians
anti.blurb: Alapin & Moscow — what most opponents play

lines.name: Najdorf (5…a6)
lines.idea: The Najdorf: …a6 keeps options flexible, prepares …e5/…e6 and …b5, and fights for the centre and the dark squares.

lines.name: Dragon (5…g6)
lines.idea: Fianchetto the dragon bishop on g7; pressure the long diagonal and the c-file while you castle and counterattack.
moves: Castle and pile on the c-file.

lines.name: Sveshnikov (4…Nf6 5…e5)
lines.idea: Accept a backward d-pawn and the d5-hole for huge piece activity and the bishop pair after …e5 and …b5.
moves: Active pieces for the d5 weakness.

lines.name: vs Alapin (2.c3)
lines.idea: Against 2.c3 hit the centre with …Nf6 and …d6/…d5. You trade off White’s extra centre pawn and reach a comfortable, near-equal game. (≈ +0.2)
moves: 2.c3 — the Alapin, building a big centre.
Pieces traded, structure healthy — fully playable for Black.

lines.name: vs Moscow (3.Bb5+)
lines.idea: After 3.Bb5+ Bd7, trade the bishop and play a solid, equal middlegame with …Nc6, …Nf6 and a timely …d5. (≈ =)

lines.name: Sicilian Defense
lines.idea: Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, gaining the open c-file and counterplay. The most popular reply to 1.e4 for players who want to win.

name: Vienna Gambit
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 — the Vienna Gambit: rip open the f-file, push e5, and attack. Sharp, sound, and full of traps.
offBook: The gambit runs on the e5 push and the open f-file — {exp} keeps it alive.
Play it slow and the pawn just matters; {exp} keeps the attack.
Off the plan — {exp} is the move.

lines.name: Accepted 3…exf4 4.e5
lines.idea: The main gambit. 4.e5! kicks the knight to g8, then you build the big centre and regain the pawn with Qe2/Qxe5 — engine-approved, White is clearly better (≈ +0.6).
moves: 3.f4 — the Vienna Gambit; offer the f-pawn.
4.e5! — the point: hit the f6-knight before Black is ready.
6.d4 — the broad centre, the pawn long forgotten.
7.Qe2! — pin the e5-pawn to the king instead of recapturing.
8.Qxe5 — pawn regained, big lead in development. White is clearly better (≈ +0.6).

lines.name: Main 3…d5 (Black’s best)
lines.idea: Black’s strongest reply: counter in the centre. After 4.fxe5 Nxe4 it’s a sharp, balanced game (≈ equal) — develop naturally and play for the initiative on the f-file.
moves: 3…d5 — the principled strike back, Black’s best.
6.d4 — grab the centre and hit the c5-bishop.
7.Bd2 — unpin; a roughly equal, double-edged middlegame (≈ 0.0).

lines.name: Greedy …g5 — h4 & Ng5! trap
lines.idea: If Black clings to the pawn with …g5, smash it: 6.h4! g4 7.Ng5! and the e6-break tears Black open. Engine says White is clearly better (≈ +0.8).
moves: 5…g5? — greedily defending f4; this is the mistake.
6.h4! — strike the over-extended pawns at once.
7.Ng5! — leap in; f7 and the open lines are the target.
9.e6! — the breakthrough; rip open the centre.
10.Bxf4 — development complete, Black’s king stuck. White is clearly better (≈ +0.8).

lines.name: Passive 3…d6
lines.idea: Black props the centre passively with …d6. Just develop — Bb5, d4, Bxf4 — and you reach a dream Vienna: a huge centre and the bishop pair (≈ +1.0).
moves: 7.Bxf4 — pawn back, both bishops out, big centre. White is clearly better (≈ +1.0).

lines.name: Natural 3…Nc6
lines.idea: A very natural move that’s simply bad: 4.fxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 chases the knight around, 6.e5 wins more space, and Bc4 finishes a crushing centre (≈ +1.4).
moves: 3…Nc6? — natural, but it walks into the steamroller.
5.d4 — hit the knight and seize the centre.
8.Bc4 — eye f7; a dream centre and a near-winning grip (≈ +1.4).

name: Irregular Openings
oneLiner: Rare first moves: a3, a4, b3, b4, c3, d3, e3, g3, g4, h3, h4, Nc3, Nh3.

lines.name: King's Pawn Opening
lines.idea: Uncommon first moves for surprise value. Most are sound enough but give Black a comfortable game if met with sensible central play.

name: King's Gambit
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.f4 — offer a pawn at once to rip open the f-file and attack.

lines.name: King's Gambit
lines.idea: White gives up a pawn for speed and an open f-file. If Black takes, build a big centre and hunt the king; if Black declines, develop fast and keep the attack.

name: Vienna Game
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 — a flexible start that can turn into a fast f4 attack.

lines.name: Vienna Game
lines.idea: Develop the knight first, keep f4 in reserve. White stays flexible: quiet development, or a sharp kingside push when Black is careless.

name: Bishop's Opening
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 — put the bishop on its best diagonal before the knight.

lines.name: Bishop's Opening
lines.idea: The bishop eyes f7 right away. White keeps options for d4 or f4 later and avoids the heavy theory of the Ruy Lopez and Italian.

name: Center Game
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 — grab the centre and bring the queen out early.

lines.name: Accepted
lines.idea: White trades the centre pawn and develops the queen fast, accepting that Black will gain tempi hitting it. Simple play, but the queen must not be careless.

name: Ponziani Opening
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3 — prepare d4 and take a big centre.

lines.name: Ponziani Opening
lines.idea: White supports a strong d4 push before Black can react. It is less known than other open games, so opponents often lack preparation.

name: Latvian Gambit
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 — an all-in counterattack with a big hole on f5.

lines.name: Latvian Gambit
lines.idea: Black attacks White's centre on move two and accepts weaknesses. Good practical chances against beginners, risky against theory.

name: Elephant Gambit
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 — hit the centre at once, even at the cost of a pawn.

lines.name: Elephant Gambit
lines.idea: Black fights for the centre immediately. It is risky against good play, so the aim is to get active pieces and punish a careless White.

name: Damiano Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 — a famous bad move; the point is to know why.

lines.name: Damiano Defense
lines.idea: 2...f6 weakens the king. Against it, White can sacrifice on e5 and win quickly. Study it to avoid, or to punish it as White.

name: Petrov Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 — mirror White's attack with a counterattack.

lines.name: Petrov Defense
lines.idea: Black attacks e4 instead of defending e5. Drawish at top level but with many traps for White who captures on e5 carelessly.

name: Philidor Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 — a solid wall of pawns and slow counterplay.

lines.name: Philidor Defense
lines.idea: Black defends e5 with a pawn, keeps a compact setup and waits. It is passive, but hard to break if you know the typical plans.

name: Scotch Game
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 — open the game right away and fight for the centre.

lines.name: Scotch Game
lines.idea: White trades the d-pawn to open lines early. Active pieces and a lead in space instead of slow manoeuvring.

name: Three Knights Game
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 — simple, solid development with both knights.

lines.name: Three Knights Game
lines.idea: Develop both knights, then choose a plan: d4, Bb5 or Bc4. A quiet way to reach a playable open game.

name: Four Knights Game
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 — symmetrical and very safe for both sides.

lines.name: Four Knights Game
lines.idea: Both sides develop all four knights. White can play the Spanish pin, or the Scotch push d4 for an open game.

name: Scandinavian Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 d5 — challenge the centre at once, queen out early.

lines.name: Scandinavian Defense
lines.idea: Black hits e4 immediately. After the exchange the queen recaptures and must be placed carefully. Few theoretical lines to learn.

name: Pirc Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 — let White build a centre, then attack it.

lines.name: Pirc Defense
lines.idea: Black fianchettos the bishop and strikes at the centre later with ...c5 or ...e5. A flexible, hypermodern defence.

name: Modern Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 g6 — fianchetto first, decide the pawn structure later.

lines.name: Modern Defense
lines.idea: Black delays the central fight and puts the bishop on g7. Very flexible, but White gets space, so react at the right time.

name: Alekhine Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 Nf6 — invite White's pawns forward, then attack them.

lines.name: Alekhine Defense
lines.idea: The knight provokes e5, and Black hopes White's advanced pawns become targets. Rich, unbalanced and tricky for both sides.

name: Nimzowitsch Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 Nc6 — develop a knight first and keep the centre flexible (includes rare side-lines).

lines.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
lines.idea: Black delays the central pawn decision and aims for ...e5 or ...d5 later. Offbeat, so it often leaves White without preparation.

name: Owen's Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 b6 — fianchetto the queen's bishop against White's centre.

lines.name: Owen's Defense
lines.idea: The bishop on b7 pressures e4 from afar. White gets space, but Black stays flexible and solid.

name: St. George Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 a6 — a tricky waiting move that prepares ...b5.

lines.name: St. George Defense
lines.idea: Black plans a queenside fianchetto and a flexible centre. Unusual, so White must think for themselves early.

name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 — take the pawn, then give it back for freedom.

lines.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
lines.idea: Black takes the c-pawn and aims for ...c5 and quick piece play. The pawn is usually returned, with an equal position.

name: Queen's Gambit Declined
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 — hold the centre with a solid pawn on e6.

lines.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
lines.idea: Black refuses the pawn and keeps the d5-pawn supported. Solid and classical, with the problem bishop on c8 to solve.

name: Semi-Slav Defense
oneLiner: 2...c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 — a sharp mix of the Slav and the QGD.

lines.name: Anti-Meran
lines.idea: Black builds a solid centre but accepts a blocked c8-bishop. The Meran and Botvinnik lines lead to very sharp, double-edged play.

name: Slav Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 — defend d5 and keep the bishop free.

lines.name: Slav Defense
lines.idea: Black supports d5 with the c-pawn and plans ...Bf5 before closing the centre with ...e6. A sturdy, reliable choice.

name: Albin Counter-Gambit
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 — sacrifice a pawn for quick activity.

lines.name: Albin Counter-Gambit
lines.idea: Black strikes at White's centre right away and gets a strong d4-pawn if White is not careful. Tricky with many traps.

name: Chigorin Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 — develop a piece and fight the centre with pieces.

lines.name: Chigorin Defense
lines.idea: Black develops the knight before the pawns and ignores classic centre rules. Unusual and rewards creative play.

name: Baltic Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 — get the bishop out early, before ...e6.

lines.name: Baltic Defense
lines.idea: Black develops the light bishop outside the pawn chain at once and keeps a solid structure.

name: London System
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 — an easy-to-learn setup that works against almost anything.

lines.name: London System
lines.idea: White develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, plays e3, c3 and Nf3. Few theory lines to memorize, with solid structure.

name: Colle System
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 — a quiet build-up before an e4 break.

lines.name: Colle System
lines.idea: White sets up pawns on d4/e3/c3, develops the bishop to d3 and prepares e4. Easy to learn, with a clear plan.

name: Torre Attack
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bg5 — pin the knight, build solidly.

lines.name: Torre Attack
lines.idea: The bishop on g5 pins the f6-knight. White follows with e3 and Nbd2, a simple system for many opponents.

name: Trompowsky Attack
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 — avoid main-line theory by attacking the knight at once.

lines.name: Trompowsky Attack
lines.idea: White pins or trades the knight to damage Black's structure and reaches unusual positions early.

name: Richter-Veresov Attack
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5 — develop actively and keep an edge in activity.

lines.name: Veresov Opening
lines.idea: White puts pieces on active squares and avoids main lines. Good for players who prefer ideas to theory.

name: Stonewall Attack
oneLiner: 1.d4 d5 and f4 — a solid pawn wall with a kingside attack.

lines.name: Dutch-style
lines.idea: White builds pawns on d4, e3, c3 and f4, then attacks on the kingside with the bishop on d3. A plan, not a list of moves.

name: Englund Gambit
oneLiner: 1.d4 e5 — a trappy gambit that sets quick tricks.

lines.name: Englund Gambit
lines.idea: Black sacrifices a pawn to bring the queen out and hunt for traps. Dangerous only if White plays carelessly.

name: Nimzo-Indian Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 — pin the knight and fight for e4.

lines.name: Nimzo-Indian Defense
lines.idea: Black develops with a pin and aims to double White's pawns. One of the soundest and most respected defences to 1.d4.

name: Queen's Indian Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 — control e4 with the bishop on b7.

lines.name: Queen's Indian Defense
lines.idea: Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop to fight for e4 and the centre. Solid and flexible.

name: Bogo-Indian Defense
oneLiner: 3.Nf3 Bb4+ — an early check that avoids the Nimzo pin theory.

lines.name: Bogo-Indian Defense
lines.idea: Black checks and trades or retreats the bishop, reaching safe positions without needing a lot of theory.

name: Catalan Opening
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 — fianchetto the bishop for long-term pressure.

lines.name: Catalan Opening
lines.idea: White's bishop on g2 presses on the long diagonal against b7 and the queenside. A strategic opening with a small, lasting edge.

name: King's Indian Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 — let White build a centre, then attack it.

lines.name: King's Indian Defense
lines.idea: Black fianchettoes and strikes with ...e5 or ...c5. Great for attacking players who like a kingside storm.

name: Grünfeld Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 — hit the centre with ...d5 at once.

lines.name: Grünfeld Defense
lines.idea: Black challenges White's centre immediately and attacks it with the bishop on g7 and ...c5. Sharp and theoretical.

name: Benko Gambit
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 — give a pawn for long-term queenside pressure.

lines.name: Benko Gambit
lines.idea: Black sacrifices the b-pawn to open files for the rooks and bishop. The pressure remains even in endgames.

name: Old Indian Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 — a solid setup with ...e5 to follow.

lines.name: Old Indian Defense
lines.idea: Black builds a compact structure and aims to strike in the centre later. Safe, if a little passive.

name: Dutch Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 f5 — fight for e4 with the f-pawn, aim for the attack.

lines.name: Dutch Defense
lines.idea: Black takes control of e4 and aims for a kingside attack. The weakened king means you must develop carefully.

name: Old Benoni Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 c5 2.d5 d6 — an older, simple way to play the Benoni.

lines.name: Old Benoni Defense
lines.idea: Black counters White's centre with the c-pawn and keeps the position flexible. White gets a space advantage.

name: English Opening
oneLiner: 1.c4 — control d5 from the flank and keep the position flexible.

lines.name: English Opening
lines.idea: White controls the centre with a flank pawn and transposes into many structures. A strategic opening for players who like flexibility.

name: Réti Opening
oneLiner: 1.Nf3 — develop first and control the centre from a distance.

lines.name: Réti Opening
lines.idea: White fianchettos and strikes in the centre later with c4. Flexible, with a hypermodern feel.

name: Bird's Opening
oneLiner: 1.f4 — seize e5 with the f-pawn and play for a kingside attack.

lines.name: Bird's Opening
lines.idea: White controls the e5 square and builds a Dutch-like setup in reverse. It weakens the king a little, but it is uncommon and surprising.

name: Nimzo-Larsen Attack
oneLiner: 1.b3 — long-diagonal pressure with the bishop on b2.

lines.name: Larsen's Opening
lines.idea: White develops the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and fights for the centre with pieces. Flexible and less studied.

name: Van Geet Opening
oneLiner: 1.Nc3 — a flexible first move that can transpose to many systems.

lines.name: Dunst Opening
lines.idea: White develops a knight first and decides on the structure later. A good surprise weapon.

name: Danish Gambit
oneLiner: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 — sacrifice pawns for two open bishops and speed.

lines.name: Declined
lines.idea: White gives one or two pawns so both bishops aim at Black's king. If Black returns the extra material correctly, White is fine; if not, the attack comes quickly.

name: Göring Gambit
oneLiner: 3.d4 exd4 4.c3 — sacrifice a pawn to open lines for the pieces.

lines.name: Declined
lines.idea: White offers a pawn for fast development and open lines against Black's king. If Black declines with ...d5, White still gets a healthy centre.

name: Lion Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 — the Philidor with a quick knight.

lines.name: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5
lines.idea: Black fights for the centre with ...e5 right away and develops the knight to d7. Solid and easy to understand.

name: Rat Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 — wait, then react to White's setup.

lines.name: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6
lines.idea: A flexible way to reach Pirc and Modern structures. Black keeps options open and avoids sharp theory.

name: Borg Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 g5 — an extreme, offbeat reply to confuse the opponent.

lines.name: 1.e4 g5
lines.idea: Black pushes the g-pawn on move one. Risky and unsound against best play, but you should know how to handle it.

name: Barnes Opening
oneLiner: 1.f3 — a weird, weakening first move; mostly a trap to avoid.

lines.name: 1.f3
lines.idea: 1.f3 blocks the knight and weakens the king. Know the dangers, and know that Black can exploit it quickly.

name: Zukertort Opening
oneLiner: 1.Nf3 followed by quiet development — flexible and often transposes.

lines.name: Zukertort Opening
lines.idea: White keeps the central structure open and decides later. Many move orders lead to well-known systems.

name: King's Indian Attack
oneLiner: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3 — one setup against almost everything.

lines.name: Smyslov Variation
lines.idea: White uses the same set-up whatever Black does, then plays e4 and attacks on the kingside. Little theory to remember.

name: Pterodactyl Defense
oneLiner: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qa5 — an offbeat queen sortie in the Sicilian.

lines.name: Pterodactyl Defense
lines.idea: Black brings the queen out early to a5 to hit e5 and the c3 square. Unusual and tricky, but White gets a lead in development.

name: English Defense
oneLiner: 1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 — queen's bishop fianchetto against d4 and c4.

lines.name: Main
lines.idea: Black aims at the centre with the bishop on b7 and keeps flexible pawn structure choices.

name: Black Knights' Tango
oneLiner: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6 — an offbeat reply that avoids main-line theory.

lines.name: Black Knights' Tango
lines.idea: Black attacks the centre with the knights before choosing a pawn structure. White gets space, but must know the tricks around ...Nb4/...Nd4.
